text: Mirela opened the tin of shoe polish. Its waxy smell brought back her father's workbench in the cellar. She stood still for a moment.
Tavish lingered over the cracked blue jug on the sill. He kept away from the stack of wet newspapers by the door.
Ottoline loved the red kite. Her brother had bought the red kite at the fair. She carried it home under her arm.
After twenty years of mending nets, Corvin's hands were quick. He tied the knot without looking.
Every morning before school Dalia fed the hens. The noise of the feed bucket barely registered with her now. Her cousin watched from the gate.
Brannoc and his sister Elowen stood by the slurry pit. The stench turned his stomach. Elowen did not seem to notice it.
Petronel turned the brass compass over in her palm twice. She set it back on the shelf and left.
Hesper spread the receipt on the counter and read it line by line: the bread, the lamp oil, a ferry ticket. She added the first two and worked out that the ferry ticket was charged twice.
Thirty winters on the ferry had taught Ansgar the sound of thin ice. The hull gave a dull knock and he knew the channel had frozen over.
Leofric could not get enough of the sour cherry jam. He ate it straight from the jar. The boiled cabbage he pushed to the edge of his plate.
Saskia hummed while she sorted the buttons by colour. The radio played quietly in the next room.
Wystan counted the crates twice. The tally matched the docket.
Rain ran down the gutter and pooled by the drain. A crate lay on its side near the kerb.
The toolkit held the old brass plumb bob, a chalk line and a folding rule.
Isolde kept drifting back to the stall with the smoked eel. She bought two fillets and ate one on the quay.
Garrick wiped the bench and hung the cloth on its nail. The kettle ticked as it cooled.
Liesel reached again for the bowl of salted almonds. The jar of pickled herring she left untouched at the far end of the table.
Old Nerys opened the drawer of the dresser. The smell of camphor brought back her aunt's wardrobe and the long winter of the flood. Nerys shut the drawer again.
A coil of wire, a spool of solder and a cracked lens lay on the bench. Dust had settled on all three.
Jorunn rinsed the brushes at the sink. Out of nowhere she thought of the blue door of the old boathouse.
Caspian stacked the chairs after the meeting. The tune of an old sea song just popped into his head.
Ysolde sat on the harbour wall while the ferry horn sounded. The word for the knot she had forgotten came to her.
Brynmor checked the three fuses in turn and ruled out the first two. So it had to be the third fuse.
